newsitem.title: INDIA: Speculation points to pilot error in air disaster.
newsitem.headline: Speculation points to pilot error in air disaster.

text.p: Speculation on the cause of the mid-air disaster which killed 349 people focused on possible pilot error on Thursday as India defended itself against charges that its flight safety equipment was outdated.

India launched an official inquiry, headed by a high court judge, into Tuesday's disaster in which two planes collided near New Delhi. "We will not spare any culprit" if any individual was to blame, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said.
But Deve Gowda, who visited the macabre crash site on Wednesday, cautioned against jumping to conclusions.

"Until the report is available, it cannot be said whether it was failure of pilots or the air traffic control," he told reporters at the crash site at Charkhi Dadri, 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi.

The Asian Age newspaper said on Thursday the onus of guilt had shifted "to either one or both of the pilots". The Times of India said preliminary indications showed the mishap was "probably due to the Kazakh pilot's error".
A Saudi Arabia Airlines jumbo jet carrying 312 people took off from New Delhi. Seven minutes later it collided with a KazAir Ilyushin IL-76 freighter that was preparing to land.
Authorities said the windscreen of the Kazakh freighter was largely intact after falling some 14,000 feet (4,270 metres) to the ground, indicating it was not a head-on crash.

Pilots were quick to denounce the government, saying authorities had dragged their feet in installing sophisticated radar equipment that would have allowed air traffic controllers to determine the altitude of both planes.
Aviation authorities had commissioned the purchase of such radar for Delhi airport in 1988.
But installation had been delayed for a mix of reasons including the failure of some equipment in tests and the need to build special facilities for the equipment, newspapers said.

Yogesh Chandra, the top civil servant in the Civil Aviation Ministry, said a new $92 million state-of-the-art air traffic control system being built by U.S. firm Raytheon for Bombay and Delhi airports would be operational by early next year.
Tourism Minister Srikanta Kumar Jena dismissed suggestions that poor safety standards or ageing radar equipment contributed to the crash.
"Our air control equipment and staff are regularly inspected (and) meet international standards," he told Reuters during an official visit to London.

Jena said the Kazakh pilot may have misunderstood instructions from air traffic controllers. "I have been told that the Kazakh pilot was ordered to stay at 15,000 feet (4,575 metres) but continued to descend," he said.
But KazAir spokesman Salir Mashanlo dismissed language as a likely cause. "The pilot spoke English," he said, referring to the international language of aviation.
KazAir has one of the worst reputations of the "babyflots", the airlines companies spawned by the collapse of Aeroflot in 1991.
Chandra said the transcript of the final exchanges between the two pilots and ground control in Delhi showed both understood their instructions to maintain altitudes 1,000 feet (300 metres) apart.
The Saudi aircraft reported it was flying at 14,000 feet (4,270 metres) while the Kazakh plane said it was at 15,000 feet (4,575 metres).
In his last recorded words, the Kazakh pilot acknowledged ground control advice that the Saudi plane was directly ahead.
"Identified traffic 12 o'clock reciprocal Saudi Boeing 747 14 miles. Report when in sight," the ground controller told him. "Kazakh 1907 -- Repeat, how many miles," the Kazakh pilot asked.

"14 miles now," said the ground controller. "Roger 1907," replied the Kazakh pilot. "Traffic is 13 miles at level 140 (14,000 feet)," said the controller. "1907," replied the Kazakh pilot in acknowledgement.
Experts said the KazAir pilot could have misconverted the altitude instructions into feet, the international norm.
Aircraft in the former Soviet Union use metres and unless they have altimeters showing altitude in both feet and metres, pilots use a table for conversion.
Chandra said there was no knowing yet what the pilots did after they last communicated with air traffic controllers.
"What the pilots did after this exchange of conversation is something that can only come out once the black boxes are decoded," he said.
